title: Stoic in love
hook: love people knowing they're mortal, and love them more

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic in failure, from the Meditations, Marcus's rule for falling short. Your line was return. Did you step back onto the path, without a speech? Day six hundred eighty-four.

Late at night, a parent stands in the doorway of a child's room. The child is asleep, one arm flung over the side of the bed. And out of nowhere, a thought arrives that parents rarely say out loud: what if something happened to them? It comes with a stab of fear, and right behind the fear, a wave of love so strong it almost hurts. Epictetus had something to say about that exact doorway, and it is hard to hear. Today: Stoic in love.
screen: `A PARENT IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHAT IF SOMETHING HAPPENED?` → `FEAR, THEN A WAVE OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the hard line. In the Handbook, section three, Epictetus says: if you kiss your child or your spouse, remind yourself that you're kissing a human being. Then, if they die, you won't be overwhelmed. In the Discourses he goes further: when you kiss your child, he says, whisper to yourself, tomorrow you may die. A student objects that it's an ill-omened thing to say. Epictetus answers: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested? It's just naming something natural. Second, the honest reaction. Some readers find this cold. Epictetus's stated aim is to protect the mind from being wrecked by loss, and some people hear it as holding back love to avoid pain. That reading is fair to his words, and it's worth saying plainly that not every reader, and not every Stoic since, accepts it. Third, another way it can land. Marcus Aurelius copied this teaching into his own notebook, the harvest reply and all. For some readers today, remembering that the people we love are mortal doesn't make the love smaller. It makes it sharper, more awake: no more assuming there'll be endless Tuesdays. Seneca, in one of his letters on grief, urges us to enjoy our friends eagerly while we have them, because we don't know how long that will be. Fourth, love them more. Put it together and you get the version the porch can leave with you: they are mortal, and they are loved. Not one instead of the other. The first is the reason to say the second out loud, today.
screen: `YOU'RE KISSING A HUMAN BEING.` · `SOME READERS FIND IT COLD.` · `MORTALITY MAKES LOVE MORE AWAKE.` · `SAY IT WHILE YOU CAN.` · then, large: `MORTAL, AND LOVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love. See their face clearly, the way they laugh, the way they walk into a room. Gently, let yourself remember that they're mortal, as you are. Notice what happens: maybe fear, maybe tenderness, maybe both. Don't push either away. Then let the love come forward. Think of one thing you've never quite said to them, or haven't said lately. Hold the words ready. The bell holds the time.
Handbook, Epictetus's short teaching text, where he says: when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a mortal human being. Today's word.
Your line: mortal, and loved. Tell the person you pictured that you love them today, in words, out loud or in writing. Day six hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly remember the mortality of those they love, and use it as a reason to express their love now; others find Epictetus's version too cold and set it aside.

original.note: Greek, Handbook 3: you are kissing a human being, a mortal.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Stoic in love holds back so it won't hurt.
what it means: remember they're mortal, and let that make you say the love out loud.
what a scholar hears: Handbook 3 says 'you kiss a human being'; Discourses 3.24.84–88 has the whispered 'tomorrow you may die' and the harvest reply; Marcus recalls it in Meditations 11.34.

notes: Enchiridion 3, Discourses 3.24.84–88 (whisper 'tomorrow you will die'; 'ears of corn reaped' reply), Meditations 11.34 paraphrased. Confirm.
Seneca Letters 63.8 (let us greedily enjoy our friends, for we know not how long) paraphrased; confirm section.
Marcus's children: several died young (of perhaps 13–14 children, a minority survived him). Kept general.
The script presents the critique of Epictetus's view fairly without endorsing either reading.
